html:
In 1773 the East India Company took for itself the sole right to buy opium grown in Bihar and Bengal. The trade it built paid for Britain's tea and led to war with China.

The poppy was grown by small farmers along the Ganges around Patna and Varanasi. Company agents gave cash advances and bound the farmer to deliver his whole crop at a fixed low price; growing poppy without a licence was a crime. Two great factories, at Patna and Ghazipur, dried the sap and packed it in mango-wood chests.

The Company sold the chests at auction in Calcutta. Private traders, British, American and Parsi, shipped them to the Chinese coast, where opium was banned, and smuggled them ashore. The silver they were paid bought tea at Canton. Exports rose from about 4,000 chests a year in 1800 to over 40,000 by 1838.

When China seized the opium in 1839, Britain went to war (see the First Opium War).

For most of the 19th century opium was the second or third largest source of the Indian government's income. Fortunes made in the trade built much of Bombay. Exports to China were ended in 1913. The Ghazipur factory still makes opium for medicine.
